source.title: Twin-Flow Generative Ranking Network for Recommendation
source.authors: Hao Guo; Erpeng Xue; Lei Huang; Shi-Chao Wang; Xiaolei Wang; Lei Wang; Jin-Peng Wang; Zeshun Li; Sheng Chen

record.file_problem: The text is a complete paper. Its title differs from the supplied title, but the DOI and paper text are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines scaling behavior in a recommendation-ranking model, a different task and metric from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study reports a scaling sweep for DFGR G-AUC and a compute-dependent choice of architecture depth. These do not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy or the parameter-and-token allocation law as specified. Comparisons of recommendation models and learning-rate schedules do not test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits recommendation-ranking G-AUC against training compute for a generative ranking transformer (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 9). That is a new setting with a result on whether a scaling law holds beyond text pretraining (V5). It has no language-model loss, extrapolation, compute-optimal parameter/token fits or fixed-parameter shape study, so V1–V4 and V6–V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but incomplete. The authors' main conclusion is that DFGR beats DLRM, MetaGR (HSTU) and other baselines in AUC/G-AUC while cutting training and inference cost. As secondary findings, they report that optimal G-AUC rises log-linearly with compute, which they call a scaling law, and that deeper architectures become optimal as compute and data increase.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a recommendation-ranking model and G-AUC versus computational complexity, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported compute-favored architecture varies with computational complexity: the preferred depth progresses from 2 to 4 to 8 layers; the 1-layer and 16-layer configurations perform suboptimally in the tested range.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched compute, the best-performing depth shifts from 2 to 4 to 8 layers as compute grows. The 1-layer model (dim 360) is worst throughout, and the 16-layer model (dim 32) lags but catches up.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommendation transformers, the compute-optimal depth-width configuration shifts toward deeper models as compute increases.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM ’25)
record.problems: The scaling result is for G-AUC in a recommendation task rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy. Numerical points for the plotted sweeps are not provided in the text, and no uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported numerical sweep points are available in the text; Figure 8's configuration results are represented by the stated qualitative findings in r2, and Figure 9's reported fitted curve and trend are in r1.

untested.parts: Power-law form in loss; scaling over several orders of magnitude; separate scaling in parameters or data; image/video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes.
All: no language-model pretraining loss is measured.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs is tested.
All: no fit of loss-minimising parameter and token counts against compute.
All: shapes are compared at fixed compute, not fixed parameter count.
All: no comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: The compute range of the scaling fit (about 1e2 to 1e3 PetaFLOPs on a log axis) and the fact that the fit covers only about one decade.

record.verdict_notes: This is a recommendation-systems paper; the scaling result is a minor section. Its 'power-law' wording does not match its log-linear fit of a bounded accuracy metric. Hoffmann and Kaplan are cited only to motivate the depth-allocation discussion. The learning-rate decay (WSD-style) result does not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out language-model pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
It does not fit small language-model runs and evaluate predictions on larger runs.
It varies recommendation-model depth and width at computational budgets and reports G-AUC, but does not measure loss-minimising parameter and token counts or fit their growth as powers of compute.
It compares depth and width configurations, but does not test architecture sensitivity at a fixed parameter count.
The study tests scaling in recommendation ranking using G-AUC, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy; it does not test the listed image/video, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer settings.
It reports recommendation ranking performance against computational complexity, not downstream-task performance predicted from language-model scale or pretraining loss.
It does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices or setups, or report curves bending away from a single power law.

rows.subject: DFGR
rows.operation_detail: Plots optimal G-AUC against computational complexity across DFGR parameter configurations and fits a curve.

conditions.value: optimal configurations under different computational complexities

rows.note: The authors state that G-AUC improves linearly as computational complexity increases on the plotted logarithmic compute axis, and describe the trend as a power law. This is a recommendation metric, not held-out pretraining loss.
rows.check: The fitted form is logarithmic (G-AUC = 0.0077·log(x) + 0.6774), not a power law in loss. The authors call it power-law, but the measure is a ranking accuracy metric, not held-out loss. The compute axis spans roughly 1e2 to 1e3 PetaFLOPs, about one order of magnitude, not several. The points are the best G-AUC across five depth-width configurations at each compute level, apparently read off training curves rather than from separately trained compute-optimal runs. There is no baseline and no uncertainty, so 'observed' overstates the match to V5.

rows.subject: DFGR
rows.operation_detail: Compares depth and width configurations under equivalent computational budgets and reports the performance-favored architecture as computational complexity increases.

conditions.value: equivalent computational budgets across the five experiments

rows.measure: G-AUC across computational complexity for different depth-width configurations
rows.value: The 1-layer configuration performed significantly worse; 16 layers were suboptimal across training phases but showed a catch-up trajectory. The optimal depth shifted from 2 to 4 to 8 layers as computational expenditure increased.
rows.note: This is an architecture-allocation finding for recommendation ranking, not a measurement of the parameter-count and token-count power laws in V3.
rows.check: The depth-width configurations are matched on compute, not on parameter count. Rough L·D² estimates range from ~16K (16×32) to ~130K (1×360), so this does not test V4. It is also not V3's parameter-token allocation. Its state relative to any version cannot be set; keep it under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: DFGR generative ranking model on the TRec industrial e-commerce dataset; G-AUC versus training compute of about 100–1000 PetaFLOPs
relationships.reason: r1: G-AUC rises steadily with compute, but as a log-linear fit in an accuracy metric over about one decade. It is not shown to be a power law in loss over several orders of magnitude, and no uncertainty is reported.
relationships.display_finding: G-AUC increased steadily with a log-linear compute fit over about 100–1000 PetaFLOPs, without establishing a power law in loss.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The study reports a scaling trend for recommendation-model G-AUC with computational complexity; row r1. This supports the extension to a different setting, but does not establish the same law for held-out cross-entropy.
